s: Under the Supremacy Clause, valid federal law displaces contrary state law.
The question is always one of congressional intent, discerned from text and structure.
A statute declares that state law is displaced; courts interpret the clause's scope.
Puerto Rico v. Franklin California Tax-Free Trust (2016) said there is no presumption against preemption when interpreting an express clause.
The federal scheme is "so pervasive" or the federal interest so dominant that Congress left no room for state supplementation.
Examples are alien registration (Hines v. Davidowitz, 1941; Arizona v. United States, 2012) and nuclear safety.
Impossibility: compliance with both is physically impossible (PLIVA v. Mensing, 2011, generic drug labels).
Obstacle: state law stands as an obstacle to the accomplishment of the full purposes and objectives of Congress (Crosby v. National Foreign Trade Council, 2000).
Several Justices criticize purpose-based obstacle preemption.

In fields of traditional state regulation, courts assume the historic police powers were not superseded unless that was Congress's "clear and manifest purpose" (Rice v. Santa Fe Elevator, 1947; Wyeth v. Levine, 2009).
Preemption requires a federal law that regulates private actors.
Anti-commandeering prevents Congress from "preempting" by ordering states what to legislate (Murphy v. NCAA).
